title: A factorial design feeding study to evaluate the effects of α‐linolenic acid (ALA) versus eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) on serum lipids in healthy adults

sections.abstract: <jats:sec> <jats:title>Background</jats:title> <jats:p>Modern diets have n‐6 to n‐3 ratios greater than 10:1, whereas some ancient diets contained higher levels of α‐linolenic acid (ALA) and a ratio of ~2:1. The benefit of taking supplements of eicosapentaenoic (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acids (DHA) on serum lipids within these background diets is little known.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Aim and Methods</jats:title> <jats:p>A factorial design approach was used to test the overall diet effect (10:1 vs. 2:1), supplement (S) effect (±EPA/DHA) and potential treatment interaction on serum lipids. A randomized cross‐over feeding trial (8‐week periods) in 24 healthy adults was conducted. Subjects consumed eucaloric diets [10:1 (Control), 2:1 (ALA; 6–7g/2400 kcal/d), 10:1+S (0.20/0.72g EPA/DHA per 2400 kcal/d), and, 2:1+S].</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Results</jats:title> <jats:p>A decrease in total cholesterol (TC) [7.7±3.3 mg/dl (P<0.01)] and apolipoprotein B (ApoB) [2.7±1.5 mg/dl (P=0.04)] was observed in changing from a 10:1 to a 2:1 diet. Taking EPA/DHA decreased triglycerides 7.6±5.5 mg/dl and increased TC (8.0±3.3 mg/dl), HDL (3.0±1.0 mg/dl), LDL (6.2±2.9 mg/dl), ApoB (4.7±1.6 mg/dl) and ApoB:ApoA1 (0.03±0.01)(all P<0.001). A synergistic effect was found for TC:HDL, which decreased more than expected (P=0.01).</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title> <jats:p>The diet ratio and EPA/DHA supplement had distinct effects on serum lipids, and, synergistic effects occurred for TC:HDL, the clinical lipid parameter with the highest predictive value for cardiovascular risk.</jats:p> </jats:sec>
